article_title: US Measles Cases Surpass All of 2025's Total With Five Months Still Left in the Year
summary: Automated checks passed; manual source-by-source verification found one direct quote attributed to Healthline that is a spliced composite of two separate source sentences rather than a verbatim match. Substance is accurate; filed as a public correction.

findings.message: Quote attributed to Healthline does not appear verbatim in the source
findings.details: The article quotes Healthline as saying: "The United States is at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which it has held for the past quarter-century." The actual Healthline source contains two distinct sentences: a summary bullet reading 'The United States is at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.' and a body sentence reading 'The United States is poised to lose its measles exemption status, which it has held for the past quarter-century.' The article's quotation splices the first clause of the bullet with the second clause of the body sentence. The substantive claim is accurate and supported by the source; only the exact quoted wording is fabricated as a composite. Filed as a corrections record.

content_preview.title: US Measles Cases Surpass All of 2025's Total With Five Months Still Left in the Year
content_preview.summary: The CDC had logged 2,318 measles cases by July 23, already above 2025's full-year total of 2,289, as national vaccination rates remain below the outbreak threshold.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The number of measles cases in the United States has surpassed the full-year total for 2025, with five months still remaining in 2026, according to [STAT News](https://www.statnews.com/2026/07/24/measles-cases-surpass-2025-total-national-vaccination-rate-now-below-key-threshold/), citing the Associated Press. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had logged 2,318 measles cases as of July 23 — the Thursday before the report's July 24 publication — [according to STAT News](ht...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-organized News-category article (757 words, within the 400-1200 range). Overview/What We Know/What We Don't Know/Analysis structure is used effectively. Tone is neutral and clinical throughout — no sensationalism despite a genuinely alarming public-health statistic. No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.source_verification: Both sources were fetched successfully by chief:review (HTTP 200) and saved as gzipped HTML snapshots in sources/2026-07/us-measles-cases-surpass-all-of-2025s-total-with-five-months-still-left-in-the-year/. I decompressed and read the full text of both snapshots (verified sha256 of decompressed content against manifest.json for both: source-0.html.gz = 0b69b3a4392f32bfd3373c825c32a1667cad57ba606c4f7718d1398372da309b matched; source-1.html.gz = a77d1793a2992bd8305571038a9edd2fd9fba67414f63584234dec3745be5472 matched). No live WebFetch fallback was needed. (1) source-0.html.gz (STAT News, 'Measles cases surpass last year's total, hit highest level in 35 years', AP byline, July 24 2026): confirms CDC logged 2,318 cases as of Thursday (July 23) per an agency update Friday (July 24), confirms 2025 total of 2,289 cases described verbatim as 'the worst year for measles in more than three decades', confirms the verbatim quote 'the U.S.'s worst year for measles since 1991', confirms MMR kindergarten coverage 92.5% (2024-25) vs 95.2% (2019-20), confirms South Carolina/Utah/Arizona outbreaks 'sickened hundreds', confirms South Carolina's 997-case outbreak described verbatim as 'the nation's largest outbreak in 35 years', confirms Utah's 700+ cases over more than a year, confirms Dr. Brannon Traxler's exact quote ('impossible to know and may vary during the course of an outbreak') and her title, confirms Dr. Varun Shetty's exact quote and title ('Texas' chief state epidemiologist'), confirms Rémy Pasco's exact quote ('there's just not much you can do about measles once you have it') and affiliation (mathematical epidemiologist, University of Colorado Boulder), confirms the Texas 2025 outbreak estimate 'nearly twice the size of the 762 known cases' verbatim, and confirms the Gaines County detail (182 probable cases unconfirmed, 414 confirmed county total). All STAT-attributed claims and quotes verified verbatim or as faithful paraphrase. (2) source-1.html.gz (Healthline, 'U.S. May Lose Measles Exemption Status As 2026 Cases Surpass Last Year', updated July 22 2026): confirms the Johns Hopkins U.S. Measles Tracker figure of 2,295 cases as of July 21 attributed correctly to Healthline/Johns Hopkins (distinct from the CDC/STAT figure of 2,318 — the two-tracker distinction the article draws is accurate and each figure is attributed to the correct tracker/outlet); confirms 'the South Carolina Department of Public Health declared the outbreak over on April 26, with 997 cases reported in Spartanburg County' verbatim, correctly attributed to Healthline; confirms Utah's Department of Health and Human Services figure of 514 measles cases in 2026 verbatim, correctly attributed to Healthline. ISSUE FOUND: the article presents a direct quotation attributed to Healthline — "The United States is at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which it has held for the past quarter-century" — that does not appear verbatim anywhere in the source. Healthline contains two related but distinct sentences: a summary bullet ('The United States is at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000.') and a body sentence ('The United States is poised to lose its measles exemption status, which it has held for the past quarter-century.'). The submission's quotation splices the first clause of the bullet with the second clause of the body sentence, producing a quotation that is presented as verbatim but does not match either source sentence exactly. The underlying substance (US elimination status at risk after ~25 years) is accurate and directly supported by the source, but the exact wording in quotation marks is a fabricated composite. This is a single, isolated quote-fidelity issue, not a substantive factual error — the correct information is filed as a correction rather than the article being rejected.
editor_notes.surpassed_2025_total_claim_check: The central claim of the article — that 2026 case counts have surpassed 2025's full-year total — is precisely supported by both sources under their respective trackers: STAT News/CDC (2,318 as of July 23 vs. 2,289 for all of 2025) and Healthline/Johns Hopkins Tracker (2,295 as of July 21 vs. 2,289 for all of 2025). Both counts are correctly attributed to their respective source/tracker throughout the article body, and the analysis section correctly frames this as two independent trackers converging on the same conclusion rather than conflating the two figures.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specific numbers, titles, dates, and paraphrased claims traced correctly to their cited source and tracker, with the one quote-fidelity exception noted above. No hallucinated statistics or invented sources.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral, sourced, and appropriately cautious about uncertainty (dedicates an entire 'What We Don't Know' section to undercount uncertainty and the unresolved PAHO determination process). No editorializing.
